articles.title: Man, 34, arrested over alleged voyeurism after pinhole cameras found at Sha Tin 24/Fitness branch
articles.description: 27th September 2026 - (Hong Kong) Police arrested a 34‑year‑old local man surnamed Fung in Sha Tin this evening on suspicion of voyeurism following the discovery of suspected pinhole cameras at the 24/7 Fitness branch on Lek Yuen Street. Officers said three changing rooms at the premises were found to contain similar devices. The suspect is being held for further enquiries, with the investigation handled by Sha Tin District Crime Squad Team Two. The case surfaced after a male member reported noticing a tiny blue light within a gap in the suspended ceiling of a single‑occupancy communal shower. Staff removed an object believed to be a covert camera and alerted police at about 5.11pm on 25th September. Responding officers subsequently found two more similar devices at the scene. It is understood the wiring was connected to the ceiling lighting circuit. Checks of other nearby branches under the same operator did not reveal further devices. 24/7 Fitness said it takes the matter seriously and apologised for the alarm caused to members, stressing it has zero tolerance for any intrusion of privacy. The company suspended the affected shower immediately, carried out a full inspection of all showers and changing rooms at the branch in the presence of police, and only reopened facilities after confirming no irregularities. The operator also conducted same‑day spot checks across all branches, focusing on concealed locations such as false ceilings and light troughs, and reported no abnormalities. It reiterated that CCTV is installed only in public areas for security and never in showers, changing rooms or toilets. The firm said staff notified police at the first opportunity and the branch manager has provided a statement. Additional measures include reviewing and strengthening daily cleaning and patrol routines, with increased inspection frequency. The company said it would share further updates in due course without prejudicing the ongoing investigation.

articles.title: Hong Kong has a voyeurism law, but not a voyeurism strategy
articles.description: 27th September 2026 - (Hong Kong) At 5.11pm on 25th September, police received a call from the 24/7 Fitness branch on Lek Yuen Street in Sha Tin. A member had noticed a gap in the false ceiling above a changing area and a small blue light inside it. He removed a panel and found a device fixed in place with black tape. Officers who followed up found similar devices in two more changing rooms and sealed three of the facility's four. Initial checks suggested the wiring had been connected to the lighting circuits above the ceiling. The case has been classified as voyeurism and passed to the Sha Tin District Crime Squad. No arrests have been made. The devices were not carried in a bag or held in a hand. They were wired into the building. Someone had access, time and a working knowledge of the ceiling void. The bathrooms serve both men and women, so the pool of potential victims is the entire membership rather than one gender. And the discovery was made by a customer, not by staff, a contractor or any inspection regime. The operator says it checked every changing room, shower and toilet across its network the same day, paying attention to false ceilings and light troughs, and found nothing further. The incident is not isolated. In March last year an aircraft maintenance worker admitted two counts of voyeurism after using a hidden camera in the shared changing room of a 24-hour gym in Tsz Wan Shan. He had recorded more than 100 videos involving some 50 victims and received 12 months in prison. This month a male primary school teacher was alleged to have twice filmed the intimate parts of two women inside a school in Aberdeen. Gyms, schools, hostels and trains are different places, but the pattern is constant. The offender chooses a setting where the target has undressed, or is about to, and where nobody is watching the watcher. Hong Kong's legal framework is newer than many realise. Until 2019, prosecutors relied on the offence of obtaining access to a computer with dishonest intent, known colloquially as the universal key, to charge people who filmed up skirts with their phones. The Court of Final Appeal ruled the offence could not be stretched to cover a person using his own device. The government legislated in response, and since 8 October 2021 the Crimes Ordinance has contained a specific voyeurism offence under section 159AAB and a separate offence of unlawful recording or observation of intimate parts under section 159AAC. Both carry a maximum of five years' imprisonment. Installing or adapting equipment or a structure to enable voyeurism is itself an offence at the same maximum, even if no footage is recovered. Publishing or threatening to publish intimate images is a fourth. Where the act occurs in public, the common law charge of outraging public decency remains available with a seven year maximum. A conviction also enters the sex offender conviction record, which can close off work involving children. On paper, the tools exist. The question is why the behaviour persists regardless. Part of the answer lies in sentencing. Defence practitioners note that the Department of Justice now almost never agrees to bind-over orders for these offences and that first offenders are sometimes jailed immediately. Yet the Tsz Wan Shan case, with 50 victims and over 100 recordings, drew 12 months against a five-year ceiling. Another part lies in detection. A pinhole camera is designed to defeat the eye. A five-year maximum deters only those who expect to be caught, and a device wired into a light circuit is built on the assumption that nobody will look. Singapore offers a comparison rather than a model. Reported voyeurism there rose 12 per cent to 476 cases in 2023, with public transport among the top three locations. Since April 2024, MRT stations have broadcast peak-hour warnings against molestation and upskirt photography, and some public toilets carry mirrors that let users see the top of their cubicle. Criminologist Razwana Begum frames this through routine activity theory, which holds that crime requires a motivated offender, a suitable target and the absence of a capable guardian. Announcements and mirrors add guardianship. She also cautions that constant warnings can breed suspicion, desensitise commuters and unsettle the people they are meant to protect. Visibility of enforcement matters as much as severity of punishment, and the message must be calibrated. Hong Kong's own record shows the cost of not calibrating. Student journalism from local university hostels has long documented the same cycle. A peeping incident in a bathroom, a survey on locking toilet doors, a split vote because locks are inconvenient, access codes that everyone knows, doors propped open, and punishments never made public so no deterrent is communicated. The Sha Tin gym is that cycle at commercial scale. Operators of changing facilities should treat ceiling voids, vents and fittings as security assets and inspect them on a logged schedule. Sentencing should weigh the number of victims and the degree of planning, and a wired installation should be treated as the aggravating factor it plainly is. And the public deserves a clear account of how often these offences are prosecuted and what sentences result, because deterrence that cannot be seen is not deterrence at all.

articles.title: Blenheim health professional jailed for covertly filming girls 144 times
articles.description: Two young girls, their family and friends have been torn apart by revelations their most private daily routines were filmed and viewed by the man they trusted. The Blenheim health professional has been sentenced to four years in prison on more than 30 charges of child sexual exploitation, with covert filming at the heart of his abuse. Several charges were representative. The man, who has permanent name suppression, filmed the victims showering and using the toilet on 144 occasions. Proof that he was present was in his zooming in and out on his victims, using a spy camera hidden in a power socket. On one occasion, he accidentally filmed himself entering the bathroom and moving a towel on a towel rail, which had covered the hidden camera. "An important observation was that you appeared to be controlling the recording as it was happening," Judge Tony Snell said the sentencing in the Nelson District Court. He said that demonstrated the motives were sexual. The man, described as having been a "high functioning member of the community", hung his head and sobbed, as he heard five of the six victims' statements read on their behalf during the hearing. One said she was shocked, sad and embarrassed. Another said knowing he had viewed her in such a way and that police had viewed the videos had also caused "immense distress". Another was left "physically sick" at knowing that the man had "captured parts of her she didn't like to look at herself". The man's former partner said the shame and sadness were so immense, they often avoided going out in public and considered leaving town. Judge Snell said the victims had been left ashamed, degraded, humiliated and terrified that people would find out what had happened to them. "They are victims of a sexual predator, which is you, which is ironic, because you blame much of this on your own experience being a victim." He was earlier found guilty at a judge-alone trial, where he maintained that, while his body might have been involved, his mind wasn't. "I'm still not quite sure you accept it was you doing this," Judge Snell said. The charges for offending over 16 months fell into three categories - knowingly making an objectionable publication, making an intimate visual recording and possessing an objectionable publication. Crown prosecutor Jackson Webber said there was no evidence the recordings were distributed or shared. Defence lawyer Hannah Stuart said the offending wouldn't have happened, if not for the long periods the man had been unwell, because of what happened to him as a child. The first tranche arose from him installing and operating a covert video camera at two properties, where he filmed the victims using the bathroom. He took a large number of screenshots from the videos. Charges of possession of child sexual exploitation material arose from him sourcing material online. In February 2023, police searched his Marlborough home and seized devices, which were assessed by a specialist forensics unit. Judge Snell said material from a phone could not be extracted until December 2024, because the passcode given to police was wrong. Almost 2700 still images were found in deleted data on an iPhone, which were screenshots from 58 videos, featuring three young girls in the bathroom, showering, using the toilet and dressing. The images were created between October 2021 and February 2022. Other charges related to 86 videos found in a recycle bin on the man's iPhone, taken using covert cameras hidden in a bathroom power socket. Judge Snell said it was notable that the total recording time of those 86 videos was 23 hours. Forty-three of the videos focused on the victims using the toilet. Charges 12-33 related to internet-sourced child exploitation material between April and December 2022, which had been repeatedly accessed. Police also found a file of images dating back several years. "It's clear from the evidence you were accessing such material back in 2015 for your own viewing," Judge Snell said. He said the offending against the victims he filmed was "shameful, exploitative conduct" and a "massive breach of trust". From an adjusted starting point of five years in prison, the man was awarded a minimal discount for his previous good character and personal circumstances, including that he had suffered abuse as a child, verified by a psychologist's report. Judge Snell also accepted that the man's remorse was genuine in part, which was ironic, when he was someone who claimed to understand the harm caused.

pendingReview.description: Police have arrested a Hong Kong man on suspicion of installing hidden pinhole cameras in a commercial gym's changing room. The 34-year-old suspect, surnamed Fung, was arrested on Sunday after a staff member at 24/7 Fitness Shatin in Lek Yuen Estate noticed the cameras and filed a police report, according to a police brief. The case has been classified as voyeurism -- an offence that carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison -- and passed on to the Shatin District Crime Unit for investigation. In a statement issued on Saturday evening, 24/7 Fitness said that it was aware police had arrested a man in connection with the incident at its Shatin Fun City location and expressed gratitude for their swift action, adding that the company will continue to assist with the investigation. Stepped up checks To ensure patrons' safety, the gym chain has suspended the suspect's membership and provided information requested by the police. It said that it has a zero-tolerance policy for any acts that violate member privacy and apologised to affected members. The statement also said that the company has implemented new procedures and stepped up checks across all branches. New equipment has been installed to inspect hidden areas in showers, changing rooms, and restrooms "to ensure members can use the facilities safely and with peace of mind," it said. According to the police brief, officers received the report at around 5pm on Friday and discovered three cameras upon arriving at the scene. The suspect was arrested two days later on Sunday. A Threads user who said he was a member at the gym posted a video of the hidden camera taped to the ceiling on Saturday, saying that he had also filed a police report. The video shows what appears to be a pinhole camera with a ribbon cable taped to a removable ceiling panel with black electrical tape.

pendingReview.title: Evil carer who was secretly filmed threatening Scots dementia patient struck off
pendingReview.description: A carer who was snared on a secret camera abusing an elderly dementia patient has been struck off. Amina Sani was recorded mocking and threatening the 81-year-old bedbound man until he was visibly distressed. Sick Sani also forcibly washed the man, including in his private parts, while another carer held his arms down whilst threatening to put him in a shower when he refused because he was scared. In the 20 minute footage the a former Merchant Navy crewman is heard screaming "no" and "leave me alone" in distress, before swearing at Sani and another carer. The two are then seen laughing at the frail pensioner. The Nigerian worker was caught when the man's daughter Su Christie installed a hidden camera in his room at Castlehill Care Home in Inverness. The footage was later part of a BBC documentary into the care home which featured other families speaking of cruelty and neglect. Sani went before the Scottish Social Services Council (SSSC) in a misconduct hearing after the footage came to light on April 10 last year. Th carer's lawyer, Namatirai Chiperem, told the hearing Sani had not been trained properly as the job was her first one since arriving in the UK However, SSSC chairman Iain Burke blasted the shocking incidents as "significant abuse of trust and power" and slammed Sani for failing to show remorse and said her actions were "fundamentally incompatible" with being a care worker. Morar Living who runs the care home denied Sani had not been given proper training and the facility - which has been renamed Morar Highland - was given a "good" grading in its most recent care inspection. During evidence at the hearing, the man's daughter Su Christie, said her father, a former merchant navy crewman, had a lifelong fear of showers due to a childhood trauma. Following the decsion to strike Sani off, the man's daughter, Ms Christie said: "You could tell by the things he was doing, the things he was saying, that his distress was growing and growing throughout that interaction and there was no attempt to bring him down or de-escalate him whatsoever. "He didn't know what was going on. He's a confused 81-year-old man living with dementia. He was frightened. "It was devastating, utterly devastating. I was in shock because, although I knew there were issues, I didn't expect to see that. It was very distressing to watch. "In a care setting, people living with dementia, like my father, should be treated with respect, dignity, and patience and courtesy. They should be treated as human beings and that's all I was asking for." SSSC chairman Iain Burke said: "It is clear throughout the video clips that you did not show any kindness or compassion to the resident. At one point you and your colleague can be seen laughing in response to something the resident says or does. "It does not appear to us to be laughing with the resident, but it appears more disrespectful in nature. We find that the resident suffered harm and you did not respect his dignity." A spokesperson for Morar Living told the BBC: "There is no truth in Amina Sani's claim that she was not trained properly by Morar. "The safety, dignity and wellbeing of our residents remains our priority, and all concerns regarding staff conduct are taken seriously and acted upon appropriately."
